core.text: On its own, in a main clause, the present subjunctive expresses what the speaker wants: **the subjunctive as a wish or gentle command (eamus = let's go; veniat = let him come)**. *Vīvāmus atque amēmus* — let us live and love; *vīvat Bacchus!* — long live Bacchus; *fīat voluntās tua* — may your will be done. First person plural is a suggestion, third person an order given at a distance, and a plain wish is 'may …'. Negative: *nē* — *nē timeās* — don't be afraid. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus optātīvus, hortātīvus, iussīvus*.
English uses *let's*, *let him*, *may*, *long live*: *let's go*, *may she recover*, *let them eat cake*.
Present subjunctive in a main clause, no ut: 'let us …', 'let him / them …', 'may …'. Negative nē.

Straight to 'you' goes **the imperative (the command form)**: *venī!* The subjunctive fills the gaps where no imperative exists — *veniat* (let him come), *veniāmus* (let's come) — and softens an order to 'you' (*veniās* — do come).

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) file all of this under one heading, the optative ('wish'), and say the force depends on who speaks to whom: to a superior it is a request (*Domine, mē adiuvēs!*), among equals a suggestion (*Amīcī, discēdāmus!*), to inferiors a command (*Servī corpus auferant!*). Grammar books split these as hortatory (let us), jussive (let him) and optative (may).

A wish can be strengthened with *utinam* (if only), and past tenses of the subjunctive make it a wish that cannot come true: *utinam Rōmae essem* — if only I were in Rome. In a question the same form asks what one is to do: *quid faciam?* — what am I to do?

teach.title: A verb that wants something
teach.say: Most verbs report a fact: *ambulāmus*, we are walking. But a verb standing on its own in a main clause (the sentence's own verb, not one tucked inside another clause), with no *ut* in front of it, can instead say what the speaker wants to happen. That is **the subjunctive as a wish or gentle command (eāmus = let's go; veniat = let him come)** — the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) used by itself. *ambulēmus* is not 'we walk' but 'let us walk'. Nothing else in the sentence carries the wanting: the verb ending does all of it.

check.ask: Is veniat reporting that he comes, or asking for him to come?

teach.title: Let us: the 'we' form
teach.say: A suggestion that takes you in with it uses the 'we' person. Put the two side by side: *labōrāmus* 'we work' has **-ā-**, *labōrēmus* 'let us work' has **-ē-**. The person ending **-mus** is the ordinary one and never changes; only the vowel in front of it does. (Verbs of other kinds take *-ā-* in that slot instead — *bibāmus*, let us drink — but the *-mus* is always the same.)

check.ask: Fill the blank with the 'let us' form of labōrō.

teach.title: Let him, let them: the third person
teach.say: For an order aimed at somebody who is not being spoken to, the same present subjunctive is used in the third person: *veniat* 'let him come', *veniant* 'let them come'. The endings are **-t** for one and **-nt** for more than one, on the same stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) the 'we' form stood on. Latin needs this because the ordinary command form only exists for the person you are speaking to: you cannot hand an order to somebody who is not there to take it.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the 'let them' form of portō.

teach.title: Saying no: nē
teach.say: The negative here is **nē**, not *nōn*: *nē timeās* 'don't be afraid', *nē lūdant* 'they are not to play'. The verb itself does not change at all — only the little word in front of it does. So *nē* at the head of a main clause (the sentence's own verb, with no *ut* or *cum* clause wrapped around it), with no verb of ordering anywhere before it, is the sign that something is being forbidden rather than denied.

check.ask: Does Nē … lūdant say that they do not play, or forbid it?

teach.title: May it happen: the plain wish
teach.say: The same third-person form can be a wish rather than an order — something the speaker has no power to command: *deī nōs servent*, 'may the gods keep us safe'. English marks this with *may*; Latin does not mark it at all. Who is being talked about is what tells you which reading to take: you can order a slave, but you can only wish at the gods.

check.ask: Tap the word that carries the wish.

teach.title: Not the imperative
teach.say: Straight to the person in front of you Latin has **the imperative (the command form)**: *venī!* 'come!'. The subjunctive is what fills in where no imperative exists — *veniat* for 'he', *eāmus* for 'we' — and it can soften an order to 'you' as well (*veniās*, 'do come'). Ask who has to act: if it is the person being spoken to, expect *venī*; if it is anybody else, expect *veniat*.

check.ask: What is eāmus here — a command form, or the subjunctive?
